Notes on walking the coast path in winter

2026-02-27 · 7 minute read · #walking

I walked the northern half of the coast path in February, from the estuary to the lighthouse, over eleven days. Most people walk it in summer, and for good reason: the cafés are open, the ferries run, and the paths are dry. I wanted to see it empty, and I mostly got my wish.

Two storms came through while I was out, one on day three and one on day eight. During the first, I sat in a bus shelter for four hours, eating cold pasta and reading a paperback someone had left behind. The second was worse, so I stayed an extra night in a guesthouse and lost a day.

Some notes, in no particular order:

  • Check the ferry timetables twice. Three of the river crossings stop running in winter, and the inland detours add up to fifteen kilometres.
  • Gaiters are not optional. The clifftop sections near the old mine were ankle-deep mud for kilometres at a time.
  • Book rooms a day ahead, not a week ahead. Plans change too often in bad weather, and most guesthouses had plenty of space.

The best day was day six, when the wind dropped and the sea went flat and grey, and I didn’t see another walker from breakfast until dusk. I counted seals instead: nineteen, most of them asleep on the rocks below the headland.

I’ve put my full route, with the places I stayed, on the walks page. If you go in winter, take a flask and a spare pair of socks, and don’t trust the forecast more than a day out.
